sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid record gang1270 and reference search (language=gang1270): three references, all doctype 'overview' (Z'graggen 1975, 1980; Claassen & McElhanon 1970); subclassification comments cite Jones 2023 (Horokoi paper, about Wasembo, not Ganglau).
sources.note: No descriptive (grammar/phonology/sketch) reference exists for Ganglau in Glottolog; Jones, Wesley Kuhron 2023 'Horokoi: a divergent member of the Rai Coast group of Madang languages' (conference paper, 51 pp., comparative) is about Horokoi/Wasembo [gsp].

sources.citation: Roberts, John R. 1997. Switch-reference in Papua New Guinea: a preliminary survey. In Andrew Pawley (ed.), Papers in Papuan Linguistics No. 3, 101-241. Pacific Linguistics A-87. Canberra: Australian National University. doi:10.15144/PL-A87.101
sources.note: Nothing on prosody. States that for the Yaganon family (with Peka, Kare, Dimir, etc.) 'we have no information' on switch-reference; the appendix table row 'Yaganon family ?SR Madang Z'graggen (1975)' cites only the wordlist classification, i.e. no grammatical source (published or SIL-internal) for any Yaganon language was known to SIL's Madang specialist in 1997.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J.A. 1980. A comparative word list of the Rai Coast languages, Madang Province, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics D-30. Canberra: ANU. xvi+196 pp. (Ganglau = list B12, ca. 300 items)
sources.note: Nothing. Introduction sec. 7 (pp. vii-viii) says only that the transcription is 'semiphonemic' and lists fluctuating sounds per language (Ganglau: none listed); no word in the list carries a stress mark and the words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the volume (a full-text search for stress/accent with scanned-spacing tolerance).

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J.A. 1975. The languages of the Madang District, Papua New Guinea. Pacific Linguistics B-41. Canberra: ANU. 162 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. pp. 13-14: Dumun differs from 'the neighbouring B12 Ganglau language in forty words out of sixty' and is treated as a separate language; Ganglau population 78 (census list). Classification, census and village lists only.

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J.A. 1975. The Madang-Adelbert Range Sub-Phylum. In S.A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study, Vol. 1: Papuan languages and the New Guinea linguistic scene, 569-612. Pacific Linguistics C-38. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 2.8.2.2.1.1.3 The Yaganon Family (p. 581): classification only ('consists of the languages Yabong, Ganglau, Saep and Bai.. The Yaganon Family is aberrant within the Rai Coast languages'); Ganglau otherwise appears only in the comparative tables. No stress/accent mention anywhere in the chapter (the volume's stress statements are in other chapters, e.g. Boazi).

sources.citation: Z'graggen, J.A. 1971. Classificatory and typological studies in languages of the Madang District. Pacific Linguistics C-19. Canberra: ANU. viii+187 pp.
sources.note: Does not cover the Rai Coast languages at all (Ganglau, Yaganon absent); its only stress remark (p. ~4) is that stress marking was omitted for the Madang-district languages it treats because 'the stress patterning has not been well established yet'. Not applicable to Ganglau.

sources.citation: Claassen, Oren R. & Kenneth A. McElhanon. 1970. Languages of the Finisterre Range. In Papers in New Guinea Linguistics 11, 45-78. Pacific Linguistics A-23. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Sec. 3.4.2 (p. 61) gives Ganglau's location, 200 speakers and a divergent Dumun-Kulilau dialect. Sec. 6.1.1 (p. 63) sketches Yaganon-family phonology (stop/nasal series, word-initial velar nasal 'observed in Ganglau', syllabic velar nasals, l/r, [h]~[s] correspondences) with no mention of stress. The syllable paragraph on p. 66 says 'In the Yaganon Family syllables may be closed by voiceless stops, p, t, k, voiced stops b, d, g, and nasals m, n and ng'; its only stress remarks are about Rawa, Yupna, Wantoat and Suroi, none about Yaganon/Ganglau.

sources.citation: Voegelin, C. F. & F. M. Voegelin. 1964. Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific Fascicle Three. Anthropological Linguistics 6(9). Bloomington: Indiana University. (ERIC microfiche ED 010 254 scan on archive.org, item micro_IA41153350_0254)
sources.note: No phonology content for Ganglau: the language is a bare name in a list (pp. 6-7 of the fascicle). The fascicle's penultimate-stress sentences that co-occur with 'Ganglau' in archive.org snippets belong to sketches of other (Austronesian) languages elsewhere in the fascicle.

sources.citation: Schmitz, Carl A. 1959. Zur Ethnologie der Rai-Kueste in Neuguinea. Anthropos 54: 27-56 [start page 27 confirmed from running head; end page approximate].
sources.note: No phonology content. Section 1 'Die Sprachgruppen' only enumerates coastal groups as Melanesian- vs non-Melanesian-speaking: 'c) oestlich anschliessend die nicht-melanesisch sprechende Gruppe: Ganglau und Dein mit dem Inland-Dorf Kubuk. Die Gruppe liegt um die Muendung des Jaganon herum, wird hier aber etwas auseinandergedrueckt durch d) das melanesisch sprechende Dorf Mindiri.' The rest is social organisation, yam feast, religion, mythology (data gathered in Pidgin at Biliau and Bongu, 1955/56). The 'keine stress-bedingten Quantitaetsverschiebungen' fragment that archive.org's snippet merge…
